sources.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
sources.access_note: openreview.net returned HTTP 403. The ICLR proceedings copy was used instead.

claims.statement: Self-RAG adds four types of reflection tokens: Retrieve, IsRel, IsSup and IsUse.
claims.excerpt: Table 1: Four types of reflection tokens used in SELF-RAG.

claims.statement: A critic model inserts reflection tokens into the training corpus offline, and the generator is trained with a standard language-model objective.
claims.excerpt: we compute critique offline and directly insert them into the training corpus, where the generator LM is trained with a standard LM objective

claims.statement: The generators are Llama2 7B and 13B. The experiments treat one sentence as a segment.
claims.excerpt: We use Llama2 7B and 13B (Touvron et al., 2023) as our generator base LM

claims.statement: Inference uses a segment-level beam search scored by a weighted linear sum of reflection-token probabilities, with soft or hard constraints.
claims.excerpt: segment-level beam search using the weighted linear sum of the reflection token probabilities as segment score

claims.statement: The authors state that the method can still generate outputs that the citations do not fully support.
claims.excerpt: it can still generate outputs that are not fully supported by the citations

claims.statement: Because the generator is trained to emit reflection tokens, the published method does not apply unchanged to a hosted model whose weights cannot be trained.
Sections 3.1 to 3.3 do not describe a task-level external record of claims, hypotheses and unverified items.

sources.title: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)

claims.statement: The strategy (no retrieval, single-step or multi-step) is selected by classifying the query's complexity before the system attempts a solution.
claims.excerpt: determining the complexity of each query before attempting a solution

claims.statement: In the multi-step strategy, retrieval at each step takes a context of earlier documents and intermediate answers as input, so later retrieval depends on what earlier steps found.
claims.location: Section 3.1 (Multi-step Approach for QA) and footnote 1, p. 7039
claims.excerpt: the additional context ci can be composed of previous documents and outcomes

claims.statement: The query-complexity classifier is a trained T5-Large model.
claims.excerpt: for the query-complexity classifier, we use and train the T5-Large model

claims.statement: Classifier training labels are constructed automatically from the outcomes of the three strategies and from inductive biases of the datasets. The authors note that labels may be wrong and that a gap remains to the ideal (oracle) classifier.
claims.excerpt: it may have the potential to label queries incorrectly despite its effectiveness

claims.statement: The paper does not describe changing the selected strategy part-way through a query when retrieved evidence conflicts.
The paper does not describe grouping retrieved documents by shared original source.

sources.title: Assisting in Writing Wikipedia-like Articles From Scratch with Large Language Models
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)

claims.statement: STORM generates N perspectives from the tables of contents of Wikipedia articles on related topics and adds a fixed basic-fact-writer perspective.
claims.excerpt: extracts the tables of contents from their corresponding Wikipedia articles

claims.statement: The perspective set is generated before the conversations start. Each perspective then guides question asking in parallel.
claims.excerpt: Each perspective p ∈ P will be utilized to guide the LLM in the process of question asking in parallel.

claims.statement: Each perspective runs a multi-turn conversation of at most M rounds between a simulated writer and a search-grounded expert. The writer's next question depends on the conversation history, so follow-up questions adapt to earlier answers.
claims.excerpt: The conversation history enables the LLM to update its understanding of the topic and ask follow-up questions.

claims.statement: The expert splits each question into search queries and applies a rule-based filter, following the Wikipedia guideline, to exclude untrustworthy sources.
claims.excerpt: the searched results will be evaluated using a rule-based filter according to

claims.statement: The authors report that collected information may be biased towards dominant Internet sources and contain promotional content, and that generated articles can link unrelated facts.
claims.excerpt: the collected information may still be biased towards dominant sources on the Internet and may contain promotional content

claims.statement: STORM is built with zero-shot prompting in the DSPy framework, without model training.
claims.excerpt: We build STORM with zero-shot prompting using the DSPy framework

claims.statement: The method description does not include a step that groups syndicated copies of one original source. The rule-based filter targets trustworthiness, not shared provenance.

sources.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
sources.author_note: The NeurIPS proceedings PDF and BibTeX list five authors. The current arXiv abstract page also lists Edward Berman.
sources.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)

claims.statement: Reflexion has three models (Actor, Evaluator, Self-Reflection) and a memory of reflections bounded to a small number of entries, usually 1 to 3.
claims.excerpt: we bound mem by a maximum number of stored experiences, Ω (usually set to 1-3)

claims.statement: The Self-Reflection model turns a binary or scalar evaluation signal and the trajectory into natural-language feedback that is added to the next trial's context.
claims.excerpt: Reflexion converts binary or scalar feedback from the environment into verbal feedback in the form of a textual summary

claims.statement: The framework accepts scalar or free-form language feedback, from external or internally simulated sources.
claims.excerpt: various types (scalar values or free-form language) and sources (external or internally simulated) of feedback signals

claims.statement: The evaluation signal in the experiments comes from exact-match grading (reasoning), pre-defined heuristics or LLM classification (decision making) and self-written unit tests (programming).
claims.excerpt: simple binary environment feedback, pre-defined heuristics for common failure cases, and self-evaluation such as binary classification using LLMs (decision-making) or self-written unit tests (programming)

claims.statement: Reflections are produced between trials and stored for the next trial. Trials repeat until the Evaluator judges the output correct, bounded by a maximum number of trials.
claims.excerpt: After each trial t, srt, is appended mem.

claims.statement: The authors list reliance on the LLM's self-evaluation (or heuristics), no formal guarantee of success and a risk of non-optimal local minima.
claims.excerpt: it may still succumb to non-optimal local minima solutions

claims.statement: Reflexion reinforces agents through linguistic feedback rather than by updating model weights.
claims.excerpt: reinforce language agents not by updating weights

claims.statement: The paper does not describe a structured record that links claims to evidence and sources, or a step that removes duplicate sources.
